claim: Hippocampal place field sequences are supported by sensory cues and network internal mechanisms.
source: Hippocampal place field sequences are supported by sensory cues and network internal mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract presenting established knowledge about hippocampal place field sequences.

claim: Sharp-wave (SPW) sequences, theta sequences, and episode field sequences are internally generated.
source: In contrast, sharp-wave (SPW) sequences, theta sequences, and episode field sequences are internally generated.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding of these sequence types.

claim: SPW sequences have been shown to support learning.
source: SPW sequences have been shown to support learning and have been assumed to also support episodic memory.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings about SPW sequences and learning.

claim: SPW sequences have been assumed to also support episodic memory.
source: SPW sequences have been shown to support learning and have been assumed to also support episodic memory.
evidence: This claim references an assumption in the field based on prior literature.

claim: SPW sequences were present in trained rats even after episodic memory was impaired.
source: Conversely, we demonstrate these SPW sequences were present in trained rats even after episodic memory was impaired and after other internal sequences – episode field and theta sequences – were eliminated.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental observations.

claim: SPW sequences were present in trained rats after episode field and theta sequences were eliminated.
source: Conversely, we demonstrate these SPW sequences were present in trained rats even after episodic memory was impaired and after other internal sequences – episode field and theta sequences – were eliminated.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental observations.

claim: SPW sequences did not support memory despite continuing to 'replay' all task-related sequences.
source: SPW sequences did not support memory despite continuing to 'replay' all task-related sequences – place- field and episode field sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing preserved replay without memory support.

claim: SPW sequences replay place-field sequences.
source: SPW sequences did not support memory despite continuing to 'replay' all task-related sequences – place- field and episode field sequences.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: SPW sequences replay episode field sequences.
source: SPW sequences did not support memory despite continuing to 'replay' all task-related sequences – place- field and episode field sequences.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Sequence replay occurred selectively during synchronous increases of population excitability -- SPWs.
source: Sequence replay occurred selectively during synchronous increases of population excitability -- SPWs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on analysis of when sequences occur.

claim: Theta sequences depended on the presence of repeated synchronized waves of excitability – theta oscillations.
source: Similarly, theta sequences depended on the presence of repeated synchronized waves of excitability – theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on observations of theta sequences.

claim: Either intermittent or rhythmic synchronized changes of excitability trigger sequential firing of neurons, which in turn supports learning and/or memory.
source: Thus, we suggest that either intermittent or rhythmic synchronized changes of excitability trigger sequential firing of neurons, which in turn supports learning and/or memory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Sequences generated in the absence of sensory cues have been observed in various cortical areas, basal ganglia, and the hippocampus.
source: Sequences generated in the absence of sensory cues have been observed in various cortical areas, basal ganglia, and the hippocampus (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Nádasdy et al., 1999; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; O'Neil et al., 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Luczak et al., 2009; Peyrache et al., 2009; Havenith et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015; Markowitz et al., 2015; Mello et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Internally generated sequences seem to support mental functions such as cognitive planning, motor planning, visual memory, and episodic memory.
source: These internally generated sequences seem to support mental functions such as cognitive planning, motor planning, visual memory, and episodic memory.
evidence: This is a statement about the proposed functions of internal sequences based on prior literature.

claim: The composition of internal sequences reflects the synaptic connectivity of the network.
source: It has been suggested that the composition of these internal sequences reflects the synaptic connectivity of the network, first, because the formation of internal sequences frequently requires learning (Gill et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012) and, second, because similar sequences can be repeated in the absence of prominent sensory cues (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015; Markowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and logical inference from those findings.

claim: The formation of internal sequences frequently requires learning.
source: It has been suggested that the composition of these internal sequences reflects the synaptic connectivity of the network, first, because the formation of internal sequences frequently requires learning (Gill et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012) and, second, because similar sequences can be repeated in the absence of prominent sensory cues (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015; Markowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Similar sequences can be repeated in the absence of prominent sensory cues.
source: It has been suggested that the composition of these internal sequences reflects the synaptic connectivity of the network, first, because the formation of internal sequences frequently requires learning (Gill et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012) and, second, because similar sequences can be repeated in the absence of prominent sensory cues (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015; Markowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus generates internal sequences that play out over the timescale of tens of milliseconds.
source: The hippocampus generates internal sequences that play out over the timescale of tens of milliseconds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hippocampal sequences.

claim: Theta sequences are generated during running.
source: Theta sequences are generated during running (Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006), and sharp-wave (SPW) sequences are generated during pauses between runs and during sleep (Nádasdy et al., 1999; Ji and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sharp-wave (SPW) sequences are generated during pauses between runs and during sleep.
source: Theta sequences are generated during running (Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006), and sharp-wave (SPW) sequences are generated during pauses between runs and during sleep (Nádasdy et al., 1999; Ji and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus produces seconds-long internal sequences during running – episode field sequences.
source: The hippocampus also produces seconds-long internal sequences during running – episode field sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Episode field sequences are formed independently of sensory cues.
source: Episode field sequences might appear to be like place field sequences (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971); but unlike place field sequences, episode field sequences are formed independently of sensory cues and only during memory tasks (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Episode field sequences are formed only during memory tasks.
source: Episode field sequences might appear to be like place field sequences (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971); but unlike place field sequences, episode field sequences are formed independently of sensory cues and only during memory tasks (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Internal sequences were generally accepted as being necessary for learning and/or episodic memory tasks such as delayed left-right alternation or radial arm maze tasks.
source: Each of these internal sequences was generally accepted as being necessary for learning and/or episodic memory tasks such as delayed left-right alternation or radial arm maze tasks.
evidence: This statement reflects the general consensus in the field based on prior literature.

claim: Elimination of SPWs impaired learning of delayed left-right alternation or radial arm maze tasks.
source: For example, elimination of SPWs impaired learning of these tasks (Girardeau et al., 2009; Dupret et al., 2010; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Jadhav et al., 2012) and elimination of theta sequences and episode field sequences was accompanied by learning impairment as well as the loss of episodic memory in well-trained animals (Robbe et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Elimination of theta sequences and episode field sequences was accompanied by learning impairment as well as the loss of episodic memory in well-trained animals.
source: For example, elimination of SPWs impaired learning of these tasks (Girardeau et al., 2009; Dupret et al., 2010; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Jadhav et al., 2012) and elimination of theta sequences and episode field sequences was accompanied by learning impairment as well as the loss of episodic memory in well-trained animals (Robbe et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One hypothesis suggests that the waking experience of animals is reactivated during SPW events and that this reactivation strengthens connections within the hippocampal network and/or transfers the newly acquired information into the cortex.
source: One hypothesis suggests that the waking experience of animals is reactivated during SPW events and that this reactivation strengthens connections within the hippocampal network and/or transfers the newly acquired information into the cortex (Buzsáki, 1986).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by a citation.

claim: Place cells tend to fire during SPWs in an order that is similar to the order in which place fields of the same cells are organized in space, a phenomenon called 'replay' of waking experience.
source: Supportive of this hypothesis, place cells tend to fire during SPWs in an order that is similar to the order in which place fields of the same cells are organized in space, a phenomenon called 'replay' of waking experience (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Nádasdy et al., 1999; Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The fast succession of firing during theta sequences might trigger synaptic plasticity.
source: Similarly, it has been suggested that the fast succession of firing during theta sequences might trigger synaptic plasticity (Skaggs et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by a citation.

claim: Medial septum (MS) inactivation strongly impairs episodic memory.
source: To address this question, we first characterized the replay of SPW sequences during an already learned episodic memory task – a delayed left-right alternation task – and then took advantage of the fact that medial septum (MS) inactivation strongly impairs episodic memory (Chrobak et al., 1989; Mizumori et al., 1990) but leaves the local-field potential SPW events intact (Buzsáki, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Medial septum (MS) inactivation leaves the local-field potential SPW events intact.
source: To address this question, we first characterized the replay of SPW sequences during an already learned episodic memory task – a delayed left-right alternation task – and then took advantage of the fact that medial septum (MS) inactivation strongly impairs episodic memory (Chrobak et al., 1989; Mizumori et al., 1990) but leaves the local-field potential SPW events intact (Buzsáki, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Under normal conditions SPW replay was not limited to sequences that were accompanied by sensory cues, that is, to place field sequences.
source: First, we show that under normal conditions SPW replay was not limited to sequences that were accompanied by sensory cues, that is, to place field sequences.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: SPW sequences also replayed episode field sequences.
source: Rather, SPW sequences also replayed episode field sequences.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Place and episode cell sequences were replayed with comparable frequency.
source: Place and episode cell sequences were replayed with comparable frequency and their replay was not biased by the current position of the animal or by the previous or future choice of the maze arm.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Replay of place and episode cell sequences was not biased by the current position of the animal or by the previous or future choice of the maze arm.
source: Place and episode cell sequences were replayed with comparable frequency and their replay was not biased by the current position of the animal or by the previous or future choice of the maze arm.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: SPW replay of both place field and episode field sequences was preserved after MS inactivation.
source: Next, we show that SPW replay of both place field and episode field sequences was preserved after MS inactivation, suggesting that SPW sequences could not support episodic memory of animals after other internal sequences such as theta and episode field sequences were eliminated.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: SPW sequences could not support episodic memory of animals after other internal sequences such as theta and episode field sequences were eliminated.
source: Next, we show that SPW replay of both place field and episode field sequences was preserved after MS inactivation, suggesting that SPW sequences could not support episodic memory of animals after other internal sequences such as theta and episode field sequences were eliminated.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing preserved SPW sequences without memory support.

claim: The replay of episode field sequences during SPWs was preserved even after the episode field sequences themselves were eliminated during wheel running.
source: Importantly, this data demonstrates that the replay of episode field sequences during SPWs was preserved even after the episode field sequences themselves were eliminated during wheel running.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: SPW sequences reflect a preserved synaptic structure of the network rather than the memory of recent events.
source: Thus, we suggest that SPW sequences reflect a preserved synaptic structure of the network rather than the memory of recent events.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Replay of place field and episode field sequences were generated exclusively during SPW events, during the short periods when the excitability of a large population of neurons suddenly increased.
source: We show that replay of place field and episode field sequences were generated exclusively during SPW events, during the short periods when the excitability of a large population of neurons suddenly increased.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: One of the effects of the MS inactivation was elimination of such synchronized changes of excitability during running (i.e., elimination of theta oscillations).
source: Interestingly, one of the effects of the MS inactivation was elimination of such synchronized changes of excitability during running (i.e., elimination of theta oscillations).
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Isolated or repetitive waves of synchronously rising and decreasing excitability among a large population of neurons are necessary to activate internally generated sequences.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that these isolated or repetitive waves of synchronously rising and decreasing excitability among a large population of neurons are necessary to activate internally generated sequences.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: 5–20% of SPW sequences were highly correlated with the sensory-cue-guided place field sequences identified in the arms of the maze (median = 9%; z-score= 3.5–9; median z-score= 4.5).
source: As shown before, 5–20% of SPW sequences were highly correlated with the sensory-cue-guided place field sequences identified in the arms of the maze (Figure 1B,C – orange/green, median = 9%; z-score= 3.5–9; median z-score= 4.5; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: About 4.3–16.7% of SPW sequences were significantly correlated with the episode field sequences (median = 10.25%; z-score= 3.1–7.8, median z-score= 4.7, p<0.01).
source: Interestingly, about 4.3–16.7% of SPW sequences were also significantly correlated with the episode field sequences (Figure 1B,C – orange/purple; median = 10.25%; z-score= 3.1–7.8, median z-score= 4.7, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: SPW sequences correlated with place or episode field sequences did not show any spatial bias.
source: SPW sequences correlated with place or episode field sequences did not show any spatial bias, suggesting they were not strongly influenced by recently traveled trajectories in the maze.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: 44.8 ± 2.9% of all SPW- sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the left maze arm were generated in the left reward area.
source: (44.8 ± 2.9% of all SPW- sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the left maze arm were generated in the left reward area . 51.2 ± 4% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the right maze arm were generated in the left reward area , n = 8 recordings from 3 animals.)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: 51.2 ± 4% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the right maze arm were generated in the left reward area.
source: (44.8 ± 2.9% of all SPW- sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the left maze arm were generated in the left reward area . 51.2 ± 4% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the right maze arm were generated in the left reward area , n = 8 recordings from 3 animals.)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: The percentage of significant sequences was not correlated with the performance of animals (Pearson correlation: Pre: r=0.34, p=0.25).
source: The percentage of significant sequences also was not correlated with the performance of animals (Pearson correlation: Pre: r=0.34, p=0.25).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Internal sequences (i.e. episode field sequences) are replayed during SPW events with equal probability as sequences strongly influenced by sensory cues (i.e. place field sequences).
source: This data shows that internal sequences (i.e. episode field sequences) are replayed during SPW events with equal probability as sequences strongly influenced by sensory cues (i.e. place field sequences).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: SPW sequences reveal synaptic structure underlying not only place field sequences but also episode field sequences.
source: This suggests that SPW sequences reveal synaptic structure underlying not only place field sequences but also episode field sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: SPW sequences do not clearly reflect an animal's most recent choices and experiences.
source: Also, this data suggests that SPW sequences do not clearly reflect an animal's most recent choices and experiences.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: SPW events were reliably generated during reward consumption and during short periods of rest in the delay area of the maze after MS inactivation.
source: SPW events were reliably generated (Figure 2A) during reward consumption and during short periods of rest in the delay area of the maze (Figure 1A-orange, 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: After MS inactivation, SPW events occurred more frequently (Kruskal-Wallis, p=5.7 * 10 e-5, n = 13).
source: After the inactivation, SPW events occurred more frequently (Figure 2C, Kruskal-Wallis, p=5.7 * 10 e-5, n = 13), recruited more neurons (Figure 2D, KS-test = 0.15; p=1.7 e-23; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997), and tended to have more spikes per neuron (Figure 2E, KS-test = 0.11; p=8.4 e-10; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997) even though the duration of the SPW events did not change (Figure 2F, KS-test = 0.08; p>> 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After MS inactivation, SPW events recruited more neurons (KS-test = 0.15; p=1.7 e-23; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997).
source: After the inactivation, SPW events occurred more frequently (Figure 2C, Kruskal-Wallis, p=5.7 * 10 e-5, n = 13), recruited more neurons (Figure 2D, KS-test = 0.15; p=1.7 e-23; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997), and tended to have more spikes per neuron (Figure 2E, KS-test = 0.11; p=8.4 e-10; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997) even though the duration of the SPW events did not change (Figure 2F, KS-test = 0.08; p>> 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After MS inactivation, SPW events tended to have more spikes per neuron (KS-test = 0.11; p=8.4 e-10; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997).
source: After the inactivation, SPW events occurred more frequently (Figure 2C, Kruskal-Wallis, p=5.7 * 10 e-5, n = 13), recruited more neurons (Figure 2D, KS-test = 0.15; p=1.7 e-23; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997), and tended to have more spikes per neuron (Figure 2E, KS-test = 0.11; p=8.4 e-10; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997) even though the duration of the SPW events did not change (Figure 2F, KS-test = 0.08; p>> 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The duration of the SPW events did not change after MS inactivation (KS-test = 0.08; p>> 0.05).
source: After the inactivation, SPW events occurred more frequently (Figure 2C, Kruskal-Wallis, p=5.7 * 10 e-5, n = 13), recruited more neurons (Figure 2D, KS-test = 0.15; p=1.7 e-23; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997), and tended to have more spikes per neuron (Figure 2E, KS-test = 0.11; p=8.4 e-10; n(Pre) = 1114; n(Musc) = 3997) even though the duration of the SPW events did not change (Figure 2F, KS-test = 0.08; p>> 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: SPW events were more frequent and stronger after MS inactivation.
source: Thus, SPW events were more frequent and stronger after MS inactivation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: SPW sequences whose orders were highly similar to the pre-inactivation episode field sequences were not eliminated by MS inactivation.
source: We found that SPW sequences whose orders were highly similar to the pre-inactivation episode field sequences were not eliminated by the inactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: After MS inactivation, a slightly higher percentage of eligible SPW sequences was significantly correlated with episode field sequences (n = 10 recordings; z-score(Pre) = 4.1 ± 0.4, z-score(Musc) = 6.7 ± 0.9; Kruskal-Wallis, p=0.023).
source: In fact, after inactivation, a slightly higher percentage of eligible SPW sequences was significantly correlated with episode field sequences (Figure 3B; n = 10 recordings; z-score(Pre) = 4.1 ± 0.4, z-score(Musc) = 6.7 ± 0.9; Kruskal-Wallis, p=0.023).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After MS inactivation, SPW sequences correlated with place field sequences were preserved (n = 8 recordings; z-score(Pre) = 5 ± 0.7; z-score(Musc) = 8.5 ± 0.9; Kruskal-Wallis, p=0.016).
source: The same held true for the SPW sequences correlated with place field sequences (Figure 3E; n = 8 recordings; z-score(Pre) = 5 ± 0.7; z-score(Musc) = 8.5 ± 0.9; Kruskal-Wallis, p=0.016).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both place and episode field sequences were replayed at close to a constant rate during the entire recording following MS inactivation.
source: Both place and episode field sequences were replayed at close to a constant rate during the entire recording following MS inactivation (Figure 3C,F), and the mean number of neurons activated during the replay of the place and episode field sequences did not change after the inactivation (Episode cells: Pre: 8.17 neurons, Musc: 8.73 neurons; Place cells: Pre: 5.96 neurons, Musc: 5.28 neurons).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figures 3C and 3F.

claim: The mean number of neurons activated during the replay of the place and episode field sequences did not change after MS inactivation (Episode cells: Pre: 8.17 neurons, Musc: 8.73 neurons; Place cells: Pre: 5.96 neurons, Musc: 5.28 neurons).
source: Both place and episode field sequences were replayed at close to a constant rate during the entire recording following MS inactivation (Figure 3C,F), and the mean number of neurons activated during the replay of the place and episode field sequences did not change after the inactivation (Episode cells: Pre: 8.17 neurons, Musc: 8.73 neurons; Place cells: Pre: 5.96 neurons, Musc: 5.28 neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Episode field sequences observed during wheel running were eliminated after MS inactivation.
source: This was the case even though the episode field sequences observed during wheel running were eliminated after MS inactivation (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the frequency of replay occurrence and the performance of animals (Pre: r = 0.34 p=0.25, Musc: r = −0.19 p=0.53).
source: Correspondingly, there was no significant correlation between the frequency of replay occurrence and the performance of animals (Figure 4A, Pre: r = 0.34 p=0.25, Musc: r = −0.19 p=0.53).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no significant decrease in the sequence replay during error trials (Correct trials: Pre: 0.22 Hz ± 0.014, Musc: 0.32 Hz ± 0.024. Error trials: Pre: 0.5 Hz ± 0.08, Musc: 0.85 Hz ± 0.25).
source: Also, we did not observe any significant decrease in the sequence replay during error trials (Figure 4B, Correct trials: Pre: 0.22 Hz ± 0.014, Musc: 0.32 Hz ± 0.024. Error trials: Pre: 0.5 Hz ± 0.08, Musc: 0.85 Hz ± 0.25).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After MS inactivation, SPW sequences that were correlated with pre-inactivation place and episode field sequences did not show clear spatial bias.
source: As before the injection, SPW sequences that were correlated with pre-inactivation place and episode field sequences did not show clear spatial bias, suggesting that they were not strongly influenced by recently traveled trajectories in the maze.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: 56 ± 6.6% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the left maze arm were generated in the left reward area after MS inactivation.
source: (56 ± 6.6% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the left maze arm were generated in the left reward area. 63 ± 8.4% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the right maze- arm were generated in the left reward area, n = 8 recordings from 3 animals).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: 63 ± 8.4% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the right maze-arm were generated in the left reward area after MS inactivation.
source: (56 ± 6.6% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the left maze arm were generated in the left reward area. 63 ± 8.4% of all SPW sequences significantly correlated with the place field sequence in the right maze- arm were generated in the left reward area, n = 8 recordings from 3 animals).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: SPW replay of episode and place field sequences does not support episodic memory in trained animals.
source: Thus, this data further confirms that SPW replay of episode and place field sequences does not support episodic memory in trained animals (Wang et al., 2015) and likely reflects the structure of the network rather than the recent activity in the network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: SPW replay likely reflects the structure of the network rather than the recent activity in the network.
source: Thus, this data further confirms that SPW replay of episode and place field sequences does not support episodic memory in trained animals (Wang et al., 2015) and likely reflects the structure of the network rather than the recent activity in the network.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Internal sequences (e.g., episode field and theta sequences) were eliminated during running after MS inactivation.
source: After MS inactivation, internal sequences (e.g., episode field and theta sequences) were eliminated during running, i.e., during theta brain state (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Highly similar sequences formed by physically identical neurons were preserved during reward consumption after MS inactivation, i.e., during SPW brain state.
source: Conversely, highly similar sequences formed by physically identical neurons were preserved during reward consumption, i.e., during SPW brain state.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Theta and SPW sequences coincide with synchronized changes in the excitability of a large population of neurons: individual troughs of theta oscillations and SPW events.
source: One common feature of the observed internal sequences (i.e., theta and SPW sequences) is that they coincide with synchronized changes in the excitability of a large population of neurons: individual troughs of theta oscillations and SPW events (Figure 5A – red traces, 4B-C; Nádasdy et al., 1999; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Theta sequences were eliminated along with the waves of excitability – theta oscillations – after MS inactivation.
source: Our previous data supports this hypothesis since theta sequences were eliminated along with the waves of excitability – theta oscillations – after MS inactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: Sequences with a similar composition to the place field and episode field sequences were not found with a probability higher than chance within a collection of 1822 time periods outside of SPW events (episode field sequence replay z-score= −0.2 ± 0.23; place field sequence replay z-score= −0.15 ± 0.25; mean: 240 ± 49 time periods per recording).
source: However, we did not find such sequences with a probability higher than chance within a collection of 1822 time periods with sufficient neuronal activity to be able to detect such sequences (Figure 5E, episode field sequence replay z-score= −0.2 ± 0.23; place field sequence replay z-score= −0.15 ± 0.25; mean: 240 ± 49 time periods per recording; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on experimental data and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both theta sequences and SPW sequences are generated exclusively at the times periods of temporally increased population excitability.
source: This data shows that both theta sequences and SPW sequences are generated exclusively at the times periods of temporally increased population excitability.
